newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Renault closure row becomes political football.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Renault closure row becomes political football.

text.p: Outrage over a decision by troubled French car maker Renault to close its Belgian assembly plant moved to the highest level of government in both countries on Friday with Belgium angrily condemning the closure.

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene told a news conference that for the Belgian government the decision to close the Vilvoorde assembly plant near Brussels with the loss of more than 3,000 jobs in July was harsh and unacceptable.

"The government is indignant and stupefied... by a brutal decision by a head office which has taken its decision far away from the locality affected and independent of its social consequences without any consultations about alternatives. This decision is unacceptable."

Dehaene took up the matter with his French counterpart Alain Juppe in a telephone conversation after the news broke late on Thursday and said that Juppe told him he would discuss the closure with the management of the partly state-owned carmaker.
The French government has 46 percent stake in Renault, which expects to have suffered its first loss in 10 years in 1996 because of weak markets, high costs and despite the launch of new models.
Dehaene said he would phone Juppe again on Monday but no meeting between the leaders was planned.
Meanwhile, top Renault management was summoned to Brussels by Luc van den Brande, the head of the regional government of Flanders, where Vilvoorde is located.

Van den Brande, who will meet Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer on Saturday, said he was "profoundly shocked by the decision, which is not based on any objective economic grounds." He called it "against all the rules of decency."
Renault said the closure was part of a wider reorganisation and would save the company 825 million French francs ($144.5 million) a year, once completed.

Dehaene said leader said the government would study Belgian, European Union and Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development rules on information and consultation of employees in such instances and consider which sanctions could be taken.
The European Commission said it was looking at the Renault case, but had no powers itself to intervene.

Belgian Labour Minister Miet Smet told Reuters that under Belgian law Renault could be fined for breaching obligations in a collective labour agreement to inform and consult employees. "The fines are calculated on a per employee basis," she said.
Outraged Vilvoorde staff occupied the plant on Thursday night, preventing finished cars from leaving the site and unions plan further protests next week.
Apart from the 3,100 staff employed at the Vilvoorde assembly plant, its closure will affect at least another 1,000 people working at supply firms and subcontractors.
French unions, fearing similar tough moves by Renault in plants in France, have called for social disobedience and set March 20 as the date for a national day of protest.
French Labour Minister Jacques Barrot tried to play down accusations in the Belgian media that Renault had opted to close a well-functioning plant in Belgium to preserve jobs in France.
"The closure of (the plant in) Belgium is not a closure against Belgium," he told French radio. ($ = 5.708 French Francs)
